en: The Scripture on the Questions of the Doubts of the Rishi Mahātejo’rcis, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of Central India during the Sui Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was staying in the city of Gayā, not long after he had attained enlightenment.

Together with all the bhikṣus and the entire assembly, some among them had attained the first fruit, others the second, and others the third or fourth fruits; according to the fruits they had attained, all their merits were entirely clear and pure.

Furthermore, there were ninety-nine billion assemblies of bodhisattvas and twenty-eight billion assemblies of devas; additionally, there were immeasurable numbers of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; sixty thousand *bala* (wrestlers) and twelve billion *nirgrantha* followers; eighty-four thousand *ṛṣis* possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*); and five hundred heterodox practitioners—all of whom smeared their bodies with ash, bared their chests, had their flesh and fat wasted away until only skin and bone remained, were hunchbacked with curved backs, wore matted hair wrapped around their heads, donned garments of tree bark, and carried jars and vases in their hands as they wandered everywhere seeking out debates on doctrine.
At that time, the World-Honored One was like Mount Sumeru standing amidst the Black Mountains, his radiance shining forth and his majestic virtue beyond compare;
the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, was likewise the most supreme among all sages.

He was like a pure white elephant with six tusks standing alone within a flock of white sheep; like the bright moon at night eclipsing the glow of all fireflies; like a mandārava flower growing amidst a marsh of reeds; and like a garuḍa dwelling among a flock of crows.
The World-Honored One was likewise among that assembly of sages, his majestic virtue and illuminating radiance being doubly more sublime.

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately entered the Jewel-Relinquishing Samādhi and manifested immeasurable supernatural powers, universally emitting pure light; his entire body shone brilliantly as rays of light intertwined and circled around him from left to right.

Furthermore, from his own body, he emanated immeasurable billions of transformation-buddha bodies, and from each of those transformation bodies, there again emerged immeasurable billions of further transformation-buddhas.

Furthermore, from within his own body, he manifested the bodies of immeasurable billions of bodhisattvas; immeasurable bodies of Śakras; immeasurable bodies of Brahmā kings; immeasurable bodies of the Four Heavenly Kings; immeasurable hundreds of thousands of arhats; immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; immeasurable bodies of great universal monarchs (cakravartins); immeasurable bodies of minor universal monarchs; immeasurable bodies of various petty kings of scattered principalities; immeasurable bodies of people from the borderlands of the eastern continent; immeasurable bodies of all people from the lands such as Southern India; and immeasurable bodies of all people belonging to the great Kṣatriya clans, the various Brāhmaṇas, and the wealthy elders.
In this way, all various forms and types, various garments and ornaments, and various modes of speech—all the various celestial realms—emerge entirely from the body of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the entire great assembly each harbored doubts and looked at one another.
Then, all the bodhisattvas were filled with great joy; they rained down various precious jewels and articles of worship, even including necklaces, as offerings to the Tathāgata.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had manifested this auspicious omen, he arose from the Jewel-Abandoning Samādhi.
Having arisen from samādhi, like a lion king stretching and looking back, he surveyed the ten directions.

Having surveyed the ten directions, he immediately beheld all the Buddha-fields throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as well as this Sahā world-system of three thousandfold worlds; observing them with the Buddha-eye, they appeared with vivid clarity, as if held in the palm of his hand.

Just as Śākyamuni Tathāgata thus manifests various transformations through the exercise of great supernormal powers, so too do all the Buddhas of the ten directions likewise manifest emanated Buddha-bodies; from these emanated bodies they further display emanated Buddha-bodies, and all those emanated Buddhas of those Tathāgatas come together like clouds to assemble at the Great Assembly of the World-Honored One.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable assemblies of bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges River and beyond all analogy—who each holding various articles of offering, approached the Buddha’s dwelling according to their respective capacities for making offerings.

Furthermore, there were great assemblies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others; having all witnessed the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers from wherever they resided, they came from those places to this ocean-like assembly.
At that time, the bodhisattvas who had come from the ten directions each made offerings to the Tathāgata with unsurpassed articles of worship.
Having completed their offerings, they each sat upon lion thrones—thrones accomplished through the six pāramitās—which were proportionate to their respective bodies;
even the humans and non-humans each sat upon thrones suited to their own bodies.
All those who were taught and transformed by Śākyamuni Tathāgata—from the Akaniṣṭha Heaven above down to the Avīci Hell below—all such transformed beings have now returned.
Having returned, at that moment, by the power of the Buddha, they all saw the worlds of the Buddhas of the ten directions as if they were a single assembly.
All those who were being taught and transformed by all the Buddhas of the ten directions entered through every pore of Śākyamuni Tathāgata;
and all those who were being taught and transformed by Śākyamuni Tathāgata entered through the pores of the bodies of those respective Buddhas.

When this manifestation had thus appeared, at that time, there was among that assembly a bodhisattva named Vijayavikrama. Rising from his seat with dignified and measured gait, his appearance majestic and serene, he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, spoke these verses:
"The Buddha’s appearance in the world is most rare; He manifests for the sake of the multitudes.
This matter has never occurred before, Overwhelming and eclipsing all Māras."
They looked at one another’s faces in turn and cried out:
“How extraordinary!
For what reason have we come?”
He spoke these words:
"We are ruined; we are pitiable, nothing remaining but our skulls and bones.
We are already emaciated; withered and aged, we have lost all joy."
The supernatural power of wordlessness and letters obscures the thorns of my path;
now the sons of the Buddha, possessing great supernatural powers, manifest the Buddha-dharma themselves.
This causes the doubting minds of these sentient beings to give rise once more to great joy.
Those in this assembly all spoke these words:
"We vow to become Buddhas.
Mañjuśrī was in the midst of the multitude, surrounded by a host of sons of the Buddha.
Mañjuśrī has attended many Buddhas; he has come to manifest and proclaim his supernormal powers.
For what dharma does he display these signs?
What dharma does the Buddha now teach?
All have conceived this doubt; I pray that you will explain it for the sake of our assembly.
At that time, within that assembly, due to the power of Māra, there was a seer named Tejaprabha who addressed the Bodhisattva Vijayavikrama, saying: “O Youth!
"You should remain silent for now; I shall now pose a question.
If this śramaṇa can resolve the doubts in my mind, only then may he be called Sarvajña;
if he cannot resolve my doubts, how can he be named 'Omniscient'?"

Such supernatural transformations may also be accomplished through the incantations taught by illusionists, Maheśvara, Nārāyaṇa, and others; for ordinary people of the world, by employing these methods, are likewise able to achieve such immeasurable feats as these.
"How could this be considered extraordinary?
As these words were spoken, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, smiled with a joyful countenance.
Having smiled, he surveyed all the sages and the entire great assembly.
Having observed the assembly, he then addressed the great seer Vidyutprabha, saying: "Vidyutprabha!
Now is the very time; ask whatever you wish, and according to my power of wisdom, I shall explain it for you."
At that time, the great seer Prabhāsa-tejas addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
Please first explain to me from where the essence of sentient beings arises."
How many are coarse?
How many are subtle?
As for the internal essential nature of sentient beings, is it one span [in height]?
Is it one foot?
Is it one finger-breadth?
Or even as much as a portion of a barley grain, a wheat grain, a large bean, or a small bean?
"Is there even as much as a mustard seed’s worth of the internal nature of sentient beings?
Having asked this, the World-Honored One then praised the great seer Vidyutprabha, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
“You, Vidyutpradīpa, have asked this matter well, as if you were one whose lifespan is sixty thousand kalpas.
When the World-Honored One spoke these words, all the sages were greatly astonished and marveled, thinking to themselves:

“We have lived together with that Great Sage for a long time in the same place, yet we still do not know the calculation of his great lifespan; how is it that this Gautama has now so quickly attained such realization?”
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the great seer Prabhāsa-tejas, saying: "O great seer!
Listen attentively and receive this well; reflect upon it thoroughly, and I shall explain it fully and correctly for you."
As for your question to me,
"From what place does the essence of sentient beings arise?
Great Seer, you should know this:
In reality, there is no speech and no words or phrases that can be spoken.

As for sentient beings having a place from which they come, it is only through the various causes and conditions such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) that those sentient beings arise; even up to the various causes and conditions such as birth, old age, sickness, and death, it is through these that those sentient beings arise.
"Great Seer!
Furthermore, there are causes and conditions that can give rise to sentient beings; that is to say, taking the mother as the cause and the father as the condition, sentient beings are born.

Moreover, the union of the parents serves as the cause, while the winds of karma—arising from improper thoughts and delusions—blow upon the seed of consciousness and place it within the womb; this is the condition."
Furthermore, the noble truth of suffering, the noble truths of its origin, its cessation, and the path—these are sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is because of the combination of the five aggregates and the eighteen elements that there are sentient beings.
Furthermore, Great Seer!
There is no karma apart from sentient beings, and there are no sentient beings apart from karma; sentient beings are karma, and karma is sentient beings.
"You should know this:
the realm of sentient beings neither increases nor decreases.
Thus spoke the Great Seer.
“Gautama! If the realm of sentient beings neither increases nor decreases, for what reason do sentient beings, having cast off their defiled bodies, obtain bodies of mastery?
The Buddha said:
"O Great Seer! What you have said is most extraordinary. Why is this so?
If one who possesses mastery were truly to possess mastery, they should never fall away and would always remain in a state of mastery;
if, however, one with a body of mastery does not possess mastery, how can they be said to have attained mastery?
"O Great Seer!
It is like a firefly that thinks to itself:
'The radiance of my flames can completely illuminate the entire Jambudvīpa.'"
"Even if a firefly were truly able to emit light that universally illuminates Jambudvīpa, it could never cause one who has not subdued the mind to be called truly self-sovereign."
Furthermore, Great Seer!
If one who possesses sovereignty were truly sovereign, he should exhaust all defilements;
because he lacks sovereignty, he should instead increase those defilements.
"If the defilements and impurities were co-existent with the sovereign [nature], then the realm of sentient beings would be seen as having neither increase nor decrease.
At that time, the Great Seer spoke again: "Gautama!
"Can you not bring all afflictions to an end?
The Buddha said, "O Great Seer!"
“I do not bring about the exhaustion of all afflictions, nor do I increase all afflictions.
The Great Seer said: “If you, Gautama, are as you say, then you should not say:”
"I have attained mastery.
The Buddha said, "Great Seer!
"So it is, so it is. Great Seer, you should know this:
I do not say, 'I have attained mastery.'"
"Why is this? Because I have no reality and am not independent.
The Great Seer said:
“Set aside that statement for now,
Gautama. Gautama,
according to what you previously said— that a sentient being is born through the union of father and mother— why is it that while many people unite, only a few sentient beings are born?”
"What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said,
"Great Seer!"
I shall now provide you with a parable; explain it for me according to your own understanding. O Great Seer!

Suppose there is a single seed from which many trees grow, and within each tree there are infinite branches, and upon each branch there are immeasurable flowers. Each of these flowers ought to produce fruit; why then is it that some bear fruit while others do not?
"If all that has already been bound were to become seeds within the process of ripening, why would there still be some that are ripe and others that are not?
What is the meaning of this?
The Great Seer replied:
“Gautama! It is because of the wind that there is ripening and non-ripening.
If it has already ripened, it falls off and does not mature; it is unfit to serve as seed.”
The Buddha told the Great Seer:
"Because the winds of karma blow upon sentient beings according to their own karma, causing them to fall into the fruits [of rebirth], there are but few sentient beings who succeed in being born."
"O Great Seer! You should know this:
if one is within the womb, they may be devoured by worms, or be broken and lost through the shifting winds of karma."
You should know this:
the number of trees that have fallen due to calamity is small and not worth mentioning; however, the number of sentient beings who have fallen due to calamity is vast and beyond description.
Furthermore, Great Seer!

Because of a distorted mind, the realm of sentient beings arises; if sentient beings were to undergo even a slight transformation of their mental conceptions, they would again receive as many future births as that number.
"Therefore, I say that it is because of a perverted mind that the realm of sentient beings arises.
At that time, the Great Seer said: "Gautama!"
"It is so, it is so. As I have asked, you have answered me, and this meaning is established.
Gautama, please explain to me further: for what reason is there the destruction by fire at the end of an eon?"
The Buddha said:
"Great Seer! You should know this:"
Because it is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*), it is called the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
If, at the time of the kalpa’s exhaustion, the great earth were not consumed by fire, the Dharma-realm would then possess two aspects:
one part would be impermanent and one part would be permanent.
If it were so, then these Tathāgatas would not be speakers of truth.
If all things were impermanent and the unconditioned dharmas were inconceivable, for this reason the Tathāgata is named the All-Knowing One.
At that time, having heard these words, the Great Seer turned his head and spoke to his own disciples, saying:
"Do you know? This Gautama has truly attained all-knowledge."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Great Immortal, saying:

"If, at the end of the kalpa, the entire great earth were not consumed by fire, one could not distinguish between this being the beginning of time and this being the end of time; nor would one know the fruits of good and evil karma, or the retributions for virtue and wickedness."
You should know this:
that which is utterly consumed and swept away during the conflagration of this kalpa is the work of the great power of skillful means of all the Tathāgatas.

Any sentient beings who are able to hear and believe that the kalpa shall be burned up and entirely engulfed in flames—beings of such number will receive the protection and guidance of all the Tathāgatas.
You should know this:
just as a great python possesses eyes, ears, a mouth, and a nose within its body, which, by the power of its venom, can capture all various kinds of flying and crawling creatures.

One should know that the Tathāgata is likewise: by means of the "poisonous power" of the methods of giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation, he is able to gather in and subdue all sentient beings.
Great Seer!

It is like a person who places a gold bar into fire—not out of anger, but because it is not yet refined and they wish to bring it to maturity; desiring to produce a genuine precious object and to obtain great wealth through its high value, they place the gold in the fire and strike it repeatedly with a hammer until it becomes supple, pure, and clear.
In this way, there are no sentient beings whatsoever who are not tamed by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, through the burning of the world at the end of the kalpa.
Thus, when the earth is consumed by fire at the end of the kalpa, in reality, there are no sentient beings who undergo suffering and affliction.
The Great Seer said:
“World-Honored One!
It is rare.”
"Is it possible that when the fire at the end of the kalpa burns and the great earth is destroyed, not a single sentient being would experience suffering?
The Buddha said, "No."
Great Seer!
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not allow a single sentient being to undergo oppression or affliction. Why is this?
"Great Seer!
For example, suppose there were fine raindrops falling from the ten directions—would those raindrops not be many?
The Great Seer replied:
“Very many,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"Great Seer! The Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are even more numerous than those.

When that kalpa ends and the great earth is consumed by fire, they remain in the space above, using the hands and bodies of their compassion, wisdom, and supernatural powers to rescue sentient beings, ensuring that no suffering touches their bodies."

Why is this? Because those Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and all Bodhisattvas possess wondrous bodies that are vast and expansive, with marks and signs that are upright and majestic; when sentient beings see them, there are none who do not rejoice and give rise to right faith, exclaiming these words:
"We vow that in future ages we shall all achieve such eradication [of suffering], and further achieve such physical forms and such bodies endowed with upright and majestic marks and signs."
At that time, there were some who, having attained liberation of mind, realized the fruit of Arhatship;
some who gave rise to a mind of weary detachment and realized the fruits of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, or Anāgāmin;
and others who attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas, or reached the stage of non-retrogression.

Some were reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; some were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven; briefly stated, there were even those who were reborn in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

"At that time, all the great universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), minor wheel-turning kings, as well as the petty kings scattered throughout various regions, the great sages (*ṛṣi*), and even the noble Kṣatriyas, the great Brāhmaṇas, and the wealthy householders—in this order, they beheld the Tathāgata’s body of wondrous form."

Furthermore, seeing that his own body has attained liberation from the great and terrifying ocean of birth and death, he gives rise to a heart of great exultation and joy, conceiving a sense of gratitude toward the Tathāgata and a desire to repay his kindness.

Having heard and received the Dharma from the Tathāgata, each of them practiced heedfulness regarding the ten paths of karmic action; by means of these skillful powers and causal conditions, they swiftly attained liberation from the ten unwholesome paths of action.

"At that time, regarding the great bodhisattvas who have attained the ten stages, as far as the range of vision of these bodhisattvas extends to illuminate the earth, the atoms of dust therein are exceedingly numerous; yet, among the realms of sentient beings during that period, those who understand the nature of afflictions as defiled and impure, and who enter the path of nirvana without remainder from within the path of unconditioned nirvana, are twice as many as those atoms."
"You should now know:
it is for the sake of such great benefits as these that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, skillfully manifest the burning up and exhaustion of the kalpa.
At that time, when all the great ṛṣis heard these words, they were struck with wonder and astonishment.
"Alas, how marvelous! How exceedingly rare!

Great Virtuous Śākyaputra, you previously addressed me as a 'Great Immortal' and extended my lifespan. Although I heard such things at that time, I still thought they were not the words of one who possesses true omniscience.
Now, having completed this gift—the most difficult of all difficulties—I have finally realized that the Śākyaputra is truly omniscient."
"I shall now address you by your true name.
At that time, all the great sages and others spoke these words:
"O Great Mass of Merit!"
O you of boundless great wisdom!
O Knower of All-Knowledge!
I observe that sentient beings hold various karmic stars that flow separately and differ from one another; where could a truly real aggregation be formed?
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me, so that I may attain awakening.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the Great Immortal, saying: “O Great Immortal!
You should know that there is no time, no direction, and no location where sentient beings can truly be gathered together.
Great Seer!

Only within equality can sentient beings be gathered; within the path of the One Vehicle can sentient beings be gathered; within the stages of the bodhisattva can sentient beings be gathered; and within the realm of nirvana without remainder can sentient beings be gathered.
You should now know this:

just as there are various streams, rivers, springs, and canals, all of which originate from various sources and flow toward the great ocean; once they have entered the great ocean, they abide in a single flavor—that is, the undifferentiated taste of salt.
"Great Seer!
You should now know this:
whatever beings in the realm of sentient beings have attained the exhaustion of outflows, they all abide in a single flavor within the taste of liberation."
You should now know this:
although I have said that sentient beings gather within the equality of afflictions, they do not truly gather. Why is this so?
For example, when a great wind swirls up, it blows together all the mosquitoes and insects that have gathered;
once the wind has subsided, they scatter in every direction.
In this same way, because all sentient beings of various kinds are bound by the winds of karma, they gather together when they fall into the hells.
Bound by the winds of karma, these beings may at times gather together among the hungry ghosts,
or they may gather together among the animals,
and so forth.
The seer spoke again:
“O Knower of All, All-Knowing One!
I pray that you will explain this to me.”
If there are such individuals as these who were born together among humans in previous lives and have now gathered together, how can they be known in the present day?
Furthermore, how can one know all those things—whether among animals or hungry ghosts—which were previously accumulated in former lives?
"I pray that you will explain this for me.
The Buddha said, "Great Seer!"

If there are sentient beings who, in a previous life, once gathered together within hell, then when they see one another in the present life, their hearts will not rejoice; they will give rise to anger, resentment, and hatred, or at times suffer headaches, or lose control of their bodily functions by urinating or defecating involuntarily. One should know that such individuals have previously gathered together within hell in a former life.
If such signs appear, one should recognize:
"He and my own body must certainly have dwelt together in one place within the hells in a previous life."
Then the Great Seer again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O All-Capable One who has realized great tranquility!
O Omniscient One!"
"Please explain this further for me:
if one has previously existed among animals, sharing a single place with ten million other bodies, how can this be known?
The Buddha told the Great Seer:
"If those individuals are born among human beings, whenever they see one another, they will form resentful enmities and constantly seek an opportunity, thinking:
'Where shall I find an opening against them?'"
This is called the sign of dwelling together in one place with many bodies among the animals; one should know that it is certain:
"I have indeed been dwelling in one place with them among the animals since long ago."

"If one has resided in a particular place among the hungry ghosts (preta), they will constantly delight in foulness and filth, and furthermore, they will have a great craving for food and breath; even if they wish to give it to others, their mind will not let go, giving rise to stinginess and attachment.
Or, seeing the wealth, nobility, and power of others, they will give rise to jealousy in their hearts, constantly desiring to obtain that person's property."
When seeing this sign, one knows for certain that they and oneself have resided together in this same place among the hungry ghosts since time immemorial.
"If there were those who previously dwelt together in the same place among humans, when they see one another again in the present life, desire arises once more."
At that time, the great seer Prabhāsa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If those who were together in the same place within the heavens in a previous life should meet one another now in the world of humans, how can they be recognized?”
The Buddha said, “Great Seer!

If there were those who were born together in the heavens in a previous life, and they now meet one another among humans, they will each perceive one another from afar through the path of the eyes and feel mutual affection.”
If these signs are present, it is certain that they have come together from among the devas.
If one observes by means of such signs, one will know the signs of the gathering of sentient beings.
At that time, having heard these words, the Great Seer was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; giving rise to a sense of rare wonder, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
Only now do I realize that those beings are truly and utterly deluded; why have they become so mired in confusion as to fail to seek and train for the sake of sarvajñā (omniscience)?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again to the Great Seer, saying:
"Great Seer, as for what you previously asked me regarding how many subtle entities exist within the bodies of sentient beings—"
If the essence of a sentient being were obtainable, that essence of a sentient being could be analyzed into parts, into subtle particles, or into long and short.
You should know this now:
it is as if there were a person born blind, and another person asked him:
"O person! What is the white color like?
What do you think?"
"Since he does not see it, can one say that 'this form is such-and-such' or 'that form is such-and-such'?
The seer replied,
"If that person does not clearly perceive the form, how would they dare to make such a definitive judgment?"
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is,
Great Seer!"
These ordinary worldlings are like those born blind; they do not see the essence of sentient beings, and thus it cannot be said:
"The subtle inner essence of such sentient beings is long or short, coarse or rough."
"Furthermore, Great Seer! The eye is not a sentient being;

the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also not sentient beings. The conditioned aggregates (skandhas) are also not sentient beings; the eighteen realms (dhātus) and the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) are also not sentient beings. Even the name 'sentient being' cannot be apprehended, nor can one obtain the designation 'sentient being' through internal emptiness, external emptiness, or internal-and-external emptiness."
Why is this? Great Seer, you should know:
the eye is a mere designation, for it does not persist even for a moment.
The provisional designations of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind do not conjoin for even a moment;
the provisional designations of the dharmas of the five aggregates do not conjoin for even a moment;
and all the provisional designations of the thirty-six kinds of impure things do not conjoin for even a moment.
In this way, there is no sentient being that can be apprehended; nor does it exist because of the mutual conjunction of the sense objects such as form and so forth.
Sentient beings are merely the various sense objects such as form, each distinct and separate, scattered and dispersed; those phenomena themselves are not the sentient being.
There is no life-force (jīva), no nourisher (poṣa); there is no master (īśvara), no person (pudgala), and likewise no self (ātman)—none of these can be apprehended.
"Furthermore, O Great Seer!
If there were such a thing as a sentient being, these Tathāgatas would not have taught the fourfold Four Noble Truths;
because in reality there is no nature of a sentient being, all Buddhas and Tathāgatas attain these dharmas, thus accord with them and thus practice them, thereby attaining the body of a Tathāgata.
At that time, the great seer Prabhāsa, desiring to attain all-knowledge, made a great and solemn vow, speaking these words:
"World-Honored One!..."
Suppose that now there were a great pit of fire, and for the duration of an entire kalpa I should dwell within it;

furthermore, suppose there were a great mountain like Mount Sumeru, its rocky cliffs steep and towering high, reaching up as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, and during that time I would cast myself down from atop it;
furthermore, suppose there were a great fire, its mass like the conflagration at the end of a kalpa—such fires with their fierce, blazing flames would scorch my body with the five heats.
The days were exceedingly long, such that a single period of time was equal to one kalpa.

During such kalpas, thirty days constituted a month, and twelve full months constituted a year; he practiced these austerities until the very end of those kalpas, joyfully and willingly enduring them, never for a moment relinquishing his diligence or failing to seek omniscience.

At that time, when the great seer Prabhāsa made these words, all the seers possessing the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā) within the great assembly rose from their seats with reverence, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and spoke thus:
"World-Honored One!..."
"From this day forward, all of us seers shall each exert ourselves with courage, diligence, and vigor, seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
After these sages had spoken these words, the World-Honored One immediately emitted various rays of light from between his eyebrows; the name of this light was "The Invincible.
Likewise, the white tufts of hair between the eyebrows of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the ten directions, emitted rays of light in the same manner.

At that time, by the power and conditions of the Buddha’s radiance, this great earth shook in six ways: namely, it moved, moved everywhere, and moved equally everywhere; it surged, surged everywhere, and surged equally everywhere; it trembled, trembled everywhere, and trembled equally everywhere; it rose, rose everywhere, and rose equally everywhere; it quaked, quaked everywhere, and quaked equally everywhere; it roared, roared everywhere, and roared equally everywhere. It surged in the east and subsided in the west; it surged in the west and subsided in the east;

it surged in the south and subsided in the north; it surged in the north and subsided in the south; it surged in the center and subsided at the edges; it surged at the edges and subsided in the center; and even its surging and subsiding above and below were likewise so.

At that time, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, from the ten directions, appeared in the void above the Buddha Śākyamuni and rained down various flowers, various exquisite incenses, and various celestial music, causing the assembly to see and hear whatever they desired according to their hearts' inclinations.

Furthermore, there were gandharva kings and immeasurable hosts of devas who all performed five kinds of music to delight the Tathāgata; moreover, from within all those musical sounds, they produced various voices of praise, chanting verses in honor of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, a gentle breeze slowly stirred these celestial fragrances, blowing them so that they hung in dense, billowing clouds, completely covering the void before the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, the great assembly of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others who had come from the ten directions leaped for joy and, each one, rained down upon the Buddha various kinds of flowers, various kinds of necklaces, various kinds of precious jewels, various kinds of blended incenses, various kinds of flower garlands, various kinds of ointments, various kinds of powdered incenses, various kinds of robes, and various kinds of banners and canopies—such immeasurable and boundless articles of offering as these—to make offerings to the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, immeasurable and boundless multitudes of devas from other directions were all filled with great joy; they likewise rained down celestial, exquisite *māndārava* flowers and *mahāmāndārava* flowers from the sky, using such various articles of offering to make offerings to the Tathāgata.

At that time, the great assembly gave rise to a sense of rare wonder; they then took the various exquisite garments they were wearing and scattered them universally over the Buddha as an offering to the Tathāgata.

At that time, an invincible great radiance and flame ascended as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven and descended as far as the Avīci hell, universally illuminating the assemblies of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, surrounding all those Tathāgatas.
Having performed this circumambulation, that great radiance came from there and returned to enter the crown of the World-Honored One’s head.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and spoke in verse:
“None of this could have occurred without the present Śākyamuni, Who has emitted wondrous light pervading all lands.
May the Buddha, out of compassion for us, And for the sake of the great assembly, speak to dispel our doubts.”
Beholding the World-Honored One manifesting his majestic countenance, some were further filled with doubt while others rejoiced;
therein, some raised one hand, leaping for joy as they praised the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Śakra, the Brahma hosts, and the Four Heavenly Kings fill the void, extolling the Buddha’s virtues;
they rain down celestial incense, flowers, and jeweled necklaces, while musical instruments produce wondrous sounds without being struck.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Elder Subhūti, saying:
"Do you now see this great seer, Tejaprabha?
Subhūti replied:
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
I have seen them; I have seen those who practice in accordance with reality.”
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Subhūti, saying: “Subhūti,
you should now know this:”

This great seer, Vidyutprabha, after the world of the thousand Buddhas of this Bhadrakalpa has passed in a future age, will again encounter an eon likewise named Bhadra; in that realm called Candrādhipati, he shall attain Buddhahood, bearing the name Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles.
“Subhūti! You should know this:
when that Tathāgata Vipaśyin appeared in the world, there were none who heard his name and did not obtain benefit, just as a wish-fulfilling jewel satisfies one’s heart’s desires.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti, you should know this:

within this assembly, eighty-four thousand rishis, having heard this Dharma-fundamental, have all attained the stage of non-retrogression. At the time of Maitreya’s descent to be born, they shall all fulfill the vows and practices of the ten stages; after three thousand kalpas have passed, they shall attain Buddhahood, with the title Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vidyotana."

Now, within this great assembly, there were further immeasurable billions of bodhisattvas who, having heard this Dharma-foundation, all attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the Samādhi of Supreme Wisdom and Majesty, the Tathāgata’s Empowerment Samādhi, the Illusion-like Samādhi, the Samādhi of the Four Elements Difficult to Subdue, the King of Mind Samādhi, the Ocean-Treasury Samādhi, the Samādhi of Subduing Adornments, the True Mind-Treasury Samādhi, and the Pure Samādhi—such as these.

Furthermore, there were multitudes of devas numbering as many as the sands of ten billion Ganges Rivers, all of whom attained the patient endurance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās all attained the fruit of arhatship.

The gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges, who had not yet resolved their minds [toward awakening], all gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Subhūti! You should now know that it is because I perceive such great benefits for these beings that I have emitted this light.”

At that time, the World-Honored One again extended his tongue-organ so that it completely covered his face. From within that tongue-organ, various colors and various radiances issued forth—namely, blue, yellow, red, white, purple, deep blue, lapis lazuli, crimson, pale gold, and crystal-colored light.
After this radiance had shone forth and reached throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions, it returned and entered back through the soles of the Tathāgata’s feet.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata does not manifest the mark of the tongue without cause or condition; we pray that the World-Honored One will explain for us what causes and what conditions have led to the manifestation of this tongue-mark and the emission of this radiance.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, saying: "Good son!

I have manifested this mark of the tongue for the sake of those sentient beings who lack faith; the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, would never utter a falsehood by means of this mark of the tongue-faculty."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If, in future ages, there are good sons or good daughters who, from within this sutra, explain even a single phrase or a single verse for others, how great will their merit be?”
“I only pray that you will explain it.
The Buddha said, “Good son!

Whatever Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, are seen by the eyes within all the Buddha-fields of the ten directions—if one were to offer all their requisites for life and articles of enjoyment to all those Buddhas, World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, continuing until they enter Great Parinirvāṇa, and even after their Parinirvāṇa, were to erect stūpas for their relics using every kind of precious object;

yet if there were another person who, from this *Tathatā-dharmamūla*, were to analyze, explain, and proclaim it to others, even a single phrase or a single verse, the merit obtained by the latter would be far greater than that.
Furthermore, good son!
If, when this Dharma-fundamental is being taught, there are those who can praise it therein, saying, "Excellent! How wonderful! you should know that all Buddhas together praise such a person.
"If there are those who make offerings to this sutra, you should know that such persons are making offerings to my very body.
At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the great assembly.
Having surveyed the great assembly, he immediately addressed them, saying:
"O sons of good family!
Wherever this sutra may be located, all Buddhas will together keep that region in their mindful recollection."
"O sons of good family!
You should know that in future ages, within Jambudvīpa, this sutra shall serve as a great panacea for all sentient beings.

If there are people who, within this sutra, either read it themselves or teach others to read it—whether once, twice, or even three times—you should know that such persons have personally requested the Tathāgata to turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma."

If there is a son of good family who, regarding this sutra, either transcribes it himself or instructs others to transcribe it, you should know that such a person is one who upholds the profound Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas; they shall constantly experience joy, swiftly attain peace and happiness, and in a future age shall attain Buddhahood.
If there are good men or good women who are destined to fall into hell, they shall never hear this subtle and wondrous sutra.
However, if those good men and good women do hear this wondrous sutra, after they cast off this body, they will certainly be reborn in a pure land.

"Furthermore, sons and daughters of good family who hear this sutra, and having heard it, rejoice, believe, delight in, and uphold it, and extensively read, recite, and explain it for others—know that such persons shall swiftly attain Bodhi; before long they will certainly have their six sense faculties complete and their five eyes purified, and at the time of death they will not forget right mindfulness."

Furthermore, they shall attain immeasurable and boundless hundreds of thousands of gates of samādhi and dhāraṇī, namely: the samādhi of entering the samādhis of all Buddhas, the samādhi of universal illumination and prowess, the samādhi of the treasury of total retention, the samādhi of the crest-jewel seal, the samādhi of the stage of empowerment, and the samādhi of the seal of contemplation;

they shall further attain the dhāraṇī of the letterless satisfaction, the dhāraṇī of the invincibility of all phenomena, the dhāraṇī of resolving doubts, and the dhāraṇī of resolving the meaning of suchness—such immeasurable and boundless hundreds of thousands of dhāraṇīs as these;
and they shall further attain the five supernormal powers, maintaining right mindfulness without confusion amidst the realms of birth and death.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “Good son!

Because you have already made offerings to immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, I entrust this Dharma to you. In future ages, you should extensively expound this fundamental teaching of the Dharma for others.”
Mañjuśrī, what do you think? Regarding all the various offerings,
various forms of respect, and various acts of welcoming you have performed in the presence of past Buddhas— can the limit of these merits be reached, or can they be measured?
Mañjuśrī said: “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said,

“Mañjuśrī! If you were to widely proclaim and disseminate such a Dharma-text as this in the future world, within this Sahā world during the age of the five corruptions, the merit you would obtain would be many times greater than that.”

Mañjuśrī! Although you have, in the presence of the World-Honored Ones of the past, provided them with various garments and the four requisites of offering so that they were always abundantly supplied, you have never yet skillfully explained this fundamental teaching for the sake of others.
For this reason, one still incurs many faults in relation to those Buddhas.

However, if you have never made offerings to even a single one of those past Buddhas, yet are able to extensively expound this profound and wondrous root of the Dharma for others, you should know that this constitutes complete and perfect offerings to all Buddhas and World-Honored Ones, and is free from any fault.

When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, Mañjuśrī and the various bodhisattvas, as well as the seer Vidyutprabha and all his retinues, along with the eight classes of devas and nāgas, the various spirits, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
The Scripture on the Questions of the Doubts of the Rishi Mahātejo’rcis-pradīpa.
